findings: ADAM uses disk-resolved SPHERE and lower-resolution complementary Keck/NIRC2 images plus optical lightcurves, with cited occultations as sanity checks. Low-resolution spherical-harmonic model is refined using SPHERE-only data and then free vertices with regularization. The inversion and claimed subpixel boundary fit are not independently reproduced.

Best-fit triaxial ellipsoid has volume-equivalent diameter 513±6 km and principal semi-axes (284×266×224)±6 km. These are model dimensions, not three diameters or directly measured local normal/radius.

Southern flattening/possible basin is explicitly unseen in the nearly pole-on SPHERE images and inferred using shape reconstruction and complementary lightcurves. About 6±1 percent volume and approximately 100000-year reorientation are model interpretations, not exposed geography or observed history.

Hydrostatic comparisons assume homogeneous or two-layer interiors. Excluding mesh below minus31 degrees gives an alternative 282×262×249 km ellipsoid; hypothetical approximately6.2h past equilibrium spin differs from approximately7.8h current rotation. No unique interior, measured ancient spin or adopted mesh is established.

Synthetic crater-density uncertainties are described as Poisson stochastic-collision uncertainties; orbital-element alternatives and impact speeds are model inputs/results, not a dated ephemeris or direct impact observation.

findings: Authors combine shape volume with literature mass to infer2.89±0.08g/cm3 bulk density. Agreement with CM grain density assumes near-zero interior porosity; it is not an independent porosity measurement or local mineral fraction.

Three-micron hydration similarity coexists with visible/near-infrared spectral differences from CM meteorites, including absent0.7–0.9micron features. Authors explicitly regard a direct CM-parent link as uncertain. Heated-CM parentage and impact-driven partial dehydration are proposed explanations, not uniquely identified composition/history.
Lower water-to-rock ratio relative to Ceres is an interpretation from density/topography/family survival. Ceres comparison does not supply Pallas geography, texture or calibrated colour.

Low versus high initial water-to-rock ratios produce distinct thermophysical pathways: undifferentiated evolved surface versus loss of a former icy shell exposing hydrated mantle. Transient ocean, shell removal and mantle exposure are conditional ancient-evolution models, not observed present ocean, active sublimation, exposed liquid or current geology.

findings.detail: Page 28 explicitly selects rows 3 and 4 of Supplementary Table 6 as better matches to the observed family size-frequency distribution. It gives excavated mass 0.016–0.027 parent-body masses, consistent with rounded row values 0.0156 and 0.0270. This selected model range is not the range of all six simulations and is not a direct measured ejecta inventory.

Excavated mass is defined before fallback using particles at r > R + 30 km, allowing target expansion. Table 6 distinguishes excavated and ejected mass. Page 29 range 0.015–0.028 and its precise quantity/selection scope remain separately recorded; page 28 does not automatically resolve every manuscript/table difference.

At least 250 km refers to a transient crater in the simulation figure, with possible later relaxation and reaccumulation. It is not an observed rim diameter, a calibrated image measurement, or an adopted surface feature.

Fragmentation duration 200 s; artificial viscosity alpha 1.5 and beta 3; N-body opening angle 0.5 rad, hexadecapole gravity, perfect merging, step 10^-6 in G=1 units over 50000 steps. These author methods were not independently reproduced. A computational tree opening angle is not a camera field of view.

Authors favour an equatorial family-forming excavation over the inferred south-pole basin. Whole-surface modification versus large-crater outcomes depend on simulated energy; neither establishes directly observed impact history or local chemistry.
